readerTitle: Your best closer might be losing you money
caseNote: 가상 사례 (청소 서비스 회사, 사내 데이터 분석팀) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 사람이 파는 방식과 고객이 혼자 사는 방식은 '어느 쪽이 더 많이 성사시키나'가 아니라 '고객 한 명을 얻는 비용이 그 고객이 남기는 돈보다 충분히 작은가'로 고른다.
misconception: 성사율이 높은 영업 방식이 언제나 더 좋은 방식이다. 사람이 직접 응대하면 무조건 더 많이 판다.

sources.text: 영업 주도(sales-led)와 셀프서브(self-serve) 판매 방식을 고객 획득 비용과 거래 규모로 비교하는 마케팅·영업 관리의 일반 개념

factChecks.note: 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 방문 견적: 방문당 $60 ÷ 성사율 50% = 고객 1명당 $120. 일반 청소 1회가 남기는 돈 $50 − $120 = −$70.
온라인 예약: 예약 1건당 광고비 $20. $50 − $20 = +$30. 이사 후 대청소: 남는 돈 $600 − 방문 견적 비용 $120 = +$480.
사내 분석팀 사례: 요청의 약 70%가 반복형 보고서라는 설정, 회의당 분석가 2시간이라는 설정은 모두 가상입니다. 계산 결과는 카드에 쓰지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Your best closer might be losing you money
body: A cleaning company's estimator visits homes and wins half of them. The new booking page wins far fewer of the people who look at it.
Everyone assumes the estimator is the better seller. The numbers say otherwise, at least for most jobs.

image.label: An estimator at a front door next to a phone showing a booking page
image.brief: 왼쪽에는 클립보드를 든 견적 담당자가 집 현관 앞에 서 있고, 오른쪽에는 스마트폰 화면에 '집 크기 선택 → 가격 → 예약' 버튼이 보임. 두 장면 사이에 저울. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: Keep the home visits?
body: Every new customer gets a free in-home estimate. Each visit costs about $60 in staff time and driving. Half of visits become customers.
A typical first job is a $160 cleaning that leaves $50 after wages and supplies. A new booking page shows fixed prices by home size. Ads cost about $20 per online booking. What do you do?

options.text: Keep visits for everyone. A 50% close rate is excellent
options.feedback: You keep the personal touch, but each customer costs more to win than the first job earns. The close rate hides the cost.

options.text: Move standard cleanings online and keep visits for big or unusual jobs
options.feedback: You stop overpaying for small jobs and still put a person where the price is hard to judge. The next card shows why.

options.text: Drop visits completely and send everyone online
options.feedback: Cheaper per customer, but you lose the large, messy jobs where customers want someone to look before they commit.

cards.title: What it costs to win one customer.
body: The visit wins more often, but each win costs **$120**. On a $50 job, that's a loss. Now take a post-renovation deep clean that leaves $600. The same $120 visit leaves $480, and the customer wants the visit before paying.
cards.softwareNote: Read the same math as cost per sign-up versus what a customer pays over time. A small monthly plan rarely covers a salesperson's calls and demos, while a large company account often does.

cards.title: Sales-led vs self-serve
body: **Sales-led** means a person guides each customer to the purchase: a quote, a visit, a call, a demo. **Self-serve** means customers learn, decide and buy on their own, from a menu, a price list or a page.
Neither is better. The rule is simple: what it costs to win one customer has to be well below what that customer leaves you. A person costs money on every deal. A good page costs money once.

cards.title: Two dials decide the motion.
body: Look at how much a sale is worth and how hard it is for the customer to decide.
list: **Small and simple:** fixed price, standard product. Self-serve.
**Big or complex:** custom price, high risk, many questions. Sales-led.
**In between:** self-serve first, with a person stepping in when a signal appears, such as a large home or an unusual request.
cards.callout: Many businesses run both, sorted by deal size.
cards.softwareNote: Software often works this way: anyone can sign up and pay by card, and accounts that add many seats get handed to a salesperson.

cards.title: Self-serve isn't free.
body: A booking page only sells when prices are clear and the product is standard. If customers have to guess, they leave quietly, and you never learn why.
You also lose conversations. An estimator hears what customers worry about. A page doesn't. Keep some way to talk to customers, even when most of them buy alone.

cards.title: Now it's a team inside a company.
body: You lead a data team that builds reports for other departments. Every request starts with a two-hour scoping meeting with an analyst. About 70% of requests are routine monthly reports. The team is always behind. What do you change?

image.label: A request form splitting into templates and a meeting room
image.brief: 사내 요청서가 두 갈래로 나뉘는 인포그래픽. 한쪽은 '보고서 템플릿' 아이콘 여러 개(셀프서브), 다른 쪽은 분석가와 마주 앉은 회의실(큰 프로젝트). 실제 회사 로고 없음.

options.text: Keep a meeting for every request so nothing gets misunderstood
options.feedback: Quality stays high, but analysts spend most of their time scoping reports that could be standard. Big projects wait.

options.text: Offer report templates people set up themselves, and meetings only for large or cross-team projects
options.feedback: Routine work moves fast, and analyst time goes where the request is costly to get wrong.

options.text: Publish templates and stop taking meetings
options.feedback: It frees the team, but complex projects get built on guesses, and fixing them later costs more than the meeting would have.

cards.title: Match how you sell to what each sale is worth.
body: A high close rate means little until you divide the cost of selling by it. Put people on big, complex deals and give everyone else a clear way to buy alone.
**Try it today:** pick your most common sale. Estimate what it costs to win one customer, then compare it with what that sale leaves behind.
